A változás értelmében a következőkre lehet még használni a régi típusú személyiket: a Magyar Államkincstár nyugellátásai, nyugdíjszerű ellátásai, pénzbeli, szociális és gyermekvédelmi ellátások átvételére; az egészségügyi szolgáltatások igénybevételére; a közszolgáltatási utazási kedvezmény érvényesítése és anyakönyvi eljárások során. A Magyarországon sokáig általánosan használt, könyv formátumú (papíralapú, puha- vagy keményfedeles) személyi igazolványok nem felelnek meg az Európai Unió okmányokra vonatkozó biztonsági minimumszabályainak. Ezek az okmányok az uniós szabályoknak való megfelelés érdekében idén augusztus 3-án érvényüket vesztették. A Belügyminisztérium a határidő lejárta előtt többször felhívta a régi típusú személyi igazolványok birtokosainak figyelmét, hogy cseréljék le ezeket az okmányokat. Mostani közleményük szerint ennek több mint 100 ezren eleget tettek, azonban még mindig 57 ezer régi típusú személyi van a lakosságnál. A Belügyminisztérium közleménye arra kéri a régi típusú személyi igazolványok birtokosait, hogy minél hamarabb cseréljék le azokat, amit bármelyik kormányablakban megtehetnek. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP View image in fullscreen A near-miss incident at Sydney airport has shone a spotlight on staff shortages for air traffic controllers. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP Transport Analysis What’s behind Sydney airport’s heavy delays and near-miss incident? Catie McLeod and Jonathan Barrett Air traffic controllers are short-staffed and exhausted – and new recruits face a difficult aptitude test and must train in Melbourne Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.01 EDT Share Travellers flying in and out of Sydney airport had already been dealing with heavy delays even before a Jetstar plane narrowly avoided colliding with a Qatar Airways plane on the tarmac early on Sunday. The day before, more than 150 flights passing through Sydney were delayed as the airport grappled with a lack of air traffic controllers, highlighting how just how delicate the rostering situation is. Two workers temporarily stood down after near-collision at Sydney airport Read more While Sunday’s incident is under investigation – an air traffic controller and a tug driver were temporarily stood down for mandatory drug and alcohol testing – the issue has shone a spotlight on the severe staffing shortages of those in charge of managing air traffic, and takeoffs and landings. ‘Doing the work of two people’ While air traffic controllers are entitled to unlimited sick leave under their terms of employment, Scott Nugent, the president of the air traffic controllers’ union Civil Air, says the issue “is that we do not have enough controllers just to fill the base roster before we have any sick leave at all”. “In practice, the only way you fill the roster is with overtime, and it relies on overtime just to do business as usual,” says Nugent. The experienced air traffic controller says workers are getting to the point where they’ve done so much overtime that they’re exhausted. Some staff are working 10 days on and then having one day off. “The reason you’ve seen these delays in the last week is because we increased the spacing between aircraft to maintain safety when we have less people,” he says. “If you’re doing the work of two people, you can only take half as many planes.” Much of the problem is tied to a pandemic-era program that incentivised a significant number of experienced staff to leave Airservices Australia, the commonwealth-owned organisation responsible for the management of the country’s skies, in 2021. With most planes grounded due to pandemic restrictions, 140 employees aged 56 or older accepted a redundancy. Soon after, the organisation embarked on a large recruitment drive but hirings have failed to keep up with demand. Gaps in rosters Despite the starting salary for a qualified air traffic controller post-training being $116,990 a year – an experienced supervisor can earn a base salary of almost $300,000 – Airservices has struggled with recruitment ever since the pandemic. In February 2024, two air traffic controllers who didn’t show up for work at Sydney airport caused cascading flight delays and cancellations across the country. Airservices narrowly avoided a similar incident in September last year. At the same time it has been trying to plug roster gaps, Airservices has been preparing for a once-in-a-generation transformation to a new flight-tracking computer system, as well as managing past allegations of workplace bullying. View image in fullscreen A plane prepares to land at Sydney airport, the busiest airport in Australia. Photograph: Izhar Khan/Reuters A review into workplace culture, conducted by the former sex discrimination commissioner Elizabeth Broderick’s firm, found 27% of staff in 2023 had experienced bullying in the past 12 months, up from 23% in 2020. From July 2022 to 2026, Airservices says it endorsed 245 controllers, most of whom qualified in 2025-2026. Over the same four-year period, 86 controllers left the organisation. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Airservices says it now has a record number of controllers across Australia. There were 985 controllers in December 2020 and 1,073 as of July this year, according to the organisation. However, the organisation says the demands on its workforce have also grown significantly, citing the new Western Sydney airport and its recent takeover of the airspace at Ballina in northern New South Wales . There still aren’t enough controllers at Sydney , Australia’s busiest airport. Tough tests and training demands A newly qualified controller can’t just fill the gap left by a retiring veteran. After 18 months of training, a newly qualified controller may be able to work in one position at a Sydney tower, such as helping organise the taxiways around the domestic airport. That person wouldn’t be qualified, for example, to work on the taxiways around the international airport, or runways, which require additional training, making newer employees less able to fill urgent vacancies. Airservices acknowledges there’s a problem. It says training experienced controllers for Sydney airport is its “top priority” but it can’t say when it will have recruited a sufficient number. Nurses sleeping in campgrounds, shops shutting and two-hour school buses: what the closure of Victoria Pass means for the Blue Mountains Read more It takes about two years to train a controller, and that’s only if someone can get past the initial screening, which includes a difficult online aptitude test as one of the first hurdles. “Only a very, very small number of people get through the application process,” says Nugent. “We’re usually talking about 2,000 people who might apply, and you hire 15 of them.” Additionally, applicants must move to Melbourne for the mandatory training. Only offering training at one location is seen as an impediment, because some applicants don’t want to relocate given there’s a risk they don’t pass. Airservices says it is considering different training locations, and says it has a new simulator in Sydney. Photograph: Jakob Fliedner/PR Movies Review Babystar review – a new arrival upends camera-ready life in disturbing family influencer satire Every ethical issue surrounding parents vlogging their kids’ childhoods for money is raised in Joscha Bongard’s debut, but it releases the dysfunctional tension too easily Cath Clarke Tue 22 Sep 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 02.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google W hen teenager Luca (Maja Bons) wants to watch the film of her birth, she finds it on YouTube. Same with the sweet, thoughtful chat her mum gave her about periods when she was nine or 10; it was filmed in the family’s podcast studio. None of life’s special moments go unmonetised in this satire from Germany , a horror story of family dysfunction. It’s a look at the dark side of the family influencer industry, raising just about every possible ethical question about parents vlogging their kids’ childhoods, and it’s impressively disturbing, up to a point. Sixteen-year-old Luca is the only child of Stella (Bea Brocks) and Chris (Liliom Lewald), social media stars who make viral videos of their perfect-looking family life for their 4 million followers. They live in a beautiful, sterile minimalist home in the countryside, and we often watch them through CCTV cameras fitted in every room. Shrewdly, first time film-maker Joscha Bongard doesn’t portray Stella and Chris as monsters; they love their daughter Luca, who they affectionately call Nunki. But fundamentally they do their best parenting in front of the camera, all bright smiles and proud affectionate glances. One day the couple tell Luca that they’re thinking about having another child. It’s hard to know what to make of this. Do they want a baby, or to increase branding opportunities with pregnancy and baby content? Their daughter hates the idea. Bons gives a brilliantly subtle performance as Luca, her face almost blank apart from twitches of tension in her cheek. Her mum wants to do a video about Luca’s feelings about the new baby; after all, personal videos get the most clicks. But Luca rebels and moves out. It’s a shame that all the tension and claustrophobia trapped in the house follows her out the door – and the last section of the film is a bit mannered by comparison.
